177.title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial
177.what: Every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed.

178.title: Place of inquiry or trial
178.what: A court can inquire into or try an offence if it was committed partly in one area and another, or if it's a continuing offence that spans multiple areas, or if the offence consists of acts done in different areas.

179.title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues
179.what: An act that is an offence because of something that was done and its consequences can be investigated or tried in a court where the action took place or the consequence occurred.

180.title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence
180.what: If an act is an offence because it relates to another offence, the court where that other offence occurred can try the case.

181.title: Place of trial in case of certain offences
181.what: Any of the following offences can be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where the accused was found: being a thug, murder committed by a thug, dacoity, dacoity with murder, gang membership, escaping from custody. Kidnapping or abduction can also be tried in a court where the person was kidnapped or abducted. Theft, extortion, robbery, and criminal misappropriation can be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where stolen property was found. Offences involving possession of stolen property can also be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where stolen property was found.

182.title: Offences committed by letters, etc
182.what: Offences that can be inquired into or tried by a specific court, including those involving cheating and property delivery, as well as offences under sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code.

183.title: Offence committed on journey or voyage
183.what: When an offence is committed whilst the person by or against whom, or the thing in respect of which, the offence is committed is in the course of performing a journey or voyage, the offence may be inquired into or tried by a Court through or into whose local jurisdiction that person or thing passed in the course of that journey or voyage.

184.title: Place of trial for offences triable together
184.what: Where— (a) the offences committed by any person are such that he may be charged with, and tried at one trial for, each such offence by virtue of the provisions of section 219, section 220 or section 221, or (b) the offence or offences committed by several persons are such that they may be charged with and tried together by virtue of the provisions of section 223, the offences may be inquired into or tried by any Court competent to inquire into or try any of the offences.

185.title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions
185.what: The State Government may direct that any cases or class of cases committed for trial in any district may be tried in any sessions division, provided such direction is not repugnant to any direction previously issued by the High Court or the Supreme Court under the Constitution, or under this Code or any other law for the time being in force.

186.title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place
186.what: If two or more courts take cognizance of the same offense, which court should inquire or try it? If they are subordinate to the same high court, that high court decides. If not, the high court with jurisdiction over the area where the first proceedings started makes the decision, and all other proceedings for that offense stop.

187.title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction
187.what: A Magistrate of the first class can issue a summons or warrant for an offence committed beyond local jurisdiction if they believe it was committed outside their jurisdiction and is triable in India under another law.

188.title: Offence committed outside India
188.what: An offence committed outside India can be dealt with as if it were committed at any place within India, but requires the previous sanction of the Central Government to be inquired into or tried in India.

189.title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India
189.what: When any offence alleged to have been committed in a territory outside India is being inquired into or tried under the provisions of section 188, the Central Government may, if it thinks fit, direct that copies of depositions made or exhibits produced before a Judicial officer in or for that territory or before a diplomatic or consular representative of India in or for that territory shall be received as evidence by the Court holding such inquiry or trial in any case in which such Court might issue a commission for taking evidence as to the matters to which such depositions or exhibits relate.

190.title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrates
190.what: A magistrate can take cognizance of an offence if they receive a complaint, police report, or information from someone else about the offence.

191.title: Transfer on application of the accused
191.what: Section 191 states that when a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 190, the accused shall be informed that he is entitled to have the case inquired into or tried by another Magistrate, and if the accused objects to further proceedings before the Magistrate taking cognizance, the case shall be transferred to such other Magistrate as may be specified by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

192.title: Making over of cases to Magistrates
192.what: Section 192 states that any Chief Judicial Magistrate may make over the case for inquiry or trial to any competent Magistrate subordinate to him, and any Magistrate of the first class empowered in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate may hold the inquiry or trial.

193.title: Cognizance of offences by Courts of Session
193.what: No Court of Session shall take cognizance of any offence as a Court of original jurisdiction unless the case has been committed to it by a Magistrate under this Code.

194.title: Additional and Assistant Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them
194.what: As Additional Sessions Judge or Assistant Sessions Judge shall try such cases as the Sessions Judge of the division may, by general or special order, make over to him for trial or as the High Court may, by special order, direct him to try.

195.title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public justice
195.what: No Court shall take cognizance of certain offences except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate.

195A.title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc
195A.what: A witness or any other person can file a complaint about an offence under this section.

196.title: Prosecution for offences against the State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such offence
196.what: No Court shall take cognizance of certain offences against the State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government or of the State Government or of the District Magistrate.

197.title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants
197.what: Section 197 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 states that no court shall take cognizance of any offence alleged to have been committed by a Judge or public servant except with the previous sanction of the Government, unless the offence is committed in connection with the affairs of the Union or State. Additionally, the provisions of sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 197 apply to all proceedings pending on the date of commencement of this Act in respect of which a Court had taken cognizance of an offence.

198.title: Prosecution for offences against marriage
198.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Chapter XX of the Indian Penal Code except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence. Exceptions include: a minor, idiot, lunatic, or woman who cannot appear in public; a husband serving in the Armed Forces with leave denied for making a complaint; or a wife whose complaint can be made on her behalf by certain relatives.

198A.title: Prosecution of offences under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code
198A.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) except upon a police report of facts which constitute such offence or upon a complaint made by the person aggrieved by the offence or by her father, mother, brother, sister or by her father’s or mother’s brother or sister or, with the leave of the Court, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption.

198B.title: Cognizance of offence
198B.what: No court can take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 376B of the Indian Penal Code if the persons involved are in a marital relationship, except if the wife files a complaint.

199.title: Prosecution for defamation
199.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Chapter XXI of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence: Provided that where such person is under the age of eighteen years, or is an idiot or a lunatic, or is from sickness or infirmity unable to make a complaint, or is a woman who, according to the local customs, ought not to be compelled to appear in public, some other person may, with the leave of the Court, make a complaint on her behalf.

200.title: Examination of complainant
200.what: A Magistrate must examine a person who files a complaint on oath, along with any present witnesses. The examination's substance will be written down and signed by all parties involved.

201.title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of the case
201.what: If the complaint is made to a Magistrate who is not competent to take cognizance of the offence, he shall return it for presentation to the proper Court with an endorsement to that effect; if the complaint is not in writing, direct the complainant to the proper Court.

202.title: Postponement of issue of process
202.what: The Magistrate may postpone the issue of process against the accused and either inquire into the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by a police officer or another person, if there is sufficient ground for proceeding.

203.title: Dismissal of complaint
203.what: If, after considering the statements on oath (if any) of the complainant and of the witnesses and the result of the inquiry or investigation (if any) under section 202, the Magistrate is of opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall dismiss the complaint, and in every such case he shall briefly record his reasons for so doing.

205.title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused
205.what: A Magistrate may dispense with the personal attendance of an accused and permit him to appear by his pleader, but the Magistrate inquiring into or trying the case may direct the personal attendance of the accused and enforce such attendance if necessary.

206.title: Special summons in cases of petty offence
206.what: A Magistrate can issue a summons to an accused in a petty offence case, requiring them to appear or plead guilty by mail, with certain conditions.

207.title: Supply to the accused of copy of police report and other documents
207.what: Section 207 states that in any case where the proceeding has been instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall without delay furnish to the accused, free of cost, a copy of each of the following documents: the police report, first information report recorded under section 154, statements recorded under sub-section (3) of section 161, confessions and statements recorded under section 164, and any other document or relevant extract thereof forwarded to the Magistrate with the police report.

208.title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by
208.what: The Magistrate must provide the accused with free copies of statements and documents if the case is triable exclusively by the Court of Session.

209.title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it
209.what: Section 209 states that when an offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the Magistrate shall commit the case to the Court of Session and remand the accused to custody until such commitment has been made.

210.title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect
210.what: When a complaint case and police investigation are happening for the same offence, the Magistrate must stop the case, get a report from the police officer, and then decide whether to try both cases together or continue with just one.

211.title: Contents of charge
211.what: Every charge under this Code shall state the offence with which the accused is charged, including the law and section of the law against which the offence is said to have been committed.

212.title: Particulars as to time, place and person
212.what: The charge must contain specific details about the time, place, person, or thing involved in the alleged offense, so the accused can understand what they are being charged with.

213.title: When manner of committing offence must be stated
213.what: When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in sections 211 and 212 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which he is charged, the charge shall also contain such particulars of the manner in which the alleged offence was committed as will be sufficient for that purpose.

214.title: Words in charge taken in sense of law under which offence is punishable
214.what: In every charge words used in describing an offence shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable.

215.title: Effect of errors
215.what: This section states that no error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded at any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice.

216.title: Court may alter charge
216.what: This section states that any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced, with certain conditions and procedures applied to ensure fairness and protection for the accused and prosecutor.

217.title: Recall of witnesses when charge altered
217.what: Whenever a charge is altered or added to by the Court after the commencement of the trial, the prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed to recall or re-summon, and examine with reference to such alteration or addition, any witness who may have been examined, unless the Court considers that this is done for vexation or delay or to defeat justice.

218.title: Separate charges for distinct offences
218.what: For every distinct offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge, and every such charge shall be tried separately: Provided that where the accused person, by an application in writing, so desires and the Magistrate is of opinion that such person is not likely to be prejudiced thereby, the Magistrate may try together all or any number of the charges framed against such person.

219.title: Three offences of same kind within year may be charged together
219.what: Three offences of the same kind committed within a year may be charged together, with a limit of three offences in total.

220.title: Trial for more than one offence
220.what: Section 220 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains that in cases where multiple offences are committed by the same person as part of the same transaction, they can be charged and tried together in a single trial for every such offence. However, if several acts combine to form different offences, the accused may be tried only once for each separate offence. This provision allows for the simultaneous trial of related offences, streamlining the legal process and reducing the burden on the court.

221.title: Where it is doubtful what offence has been committed
221.what: If a single act or series of acts is of such a nature that it is doubtful which of several offences the facts which can be proved will constitute, the accused may be charged with having committed all or any of such offences, and any number of such charges may be tried at once; or he may be charged in the alternative with having committed some one of the said offences.

222.title: When offence proved included in offence charged
222.what: When a person can be convicted of a lesser offence if some but not all of the charged offence's particulars are proved, or if the facts prove the offence is less serious than charged.

223.title: What persons may be charged jointly
223.what: The following persons may be charged and tried together: (a) those accused of the same offence in the same transaction; (b) those accused of an offence and abetment or attempt to commit it; (c) those accused of multiple offences of the same kind committed jointly within 12 months; (d) those accused of different offences in the same transaction; (e) those accused of theft, extortion, etc. and related crimes such as receiving stolen property or assisting in its disposal; (f) those accused of offences under sections 411 and 414 of the Indian Penal Code relating to stolen property; (g) those accused of counterfeit coin-related offences and other similar offences, with provisions from Chapter XII of the Indian Penal Code applying where applicable.

224.title: Withdrawal of remaining charges on conviction on one of several charges
224.what: When a charge containing more heads than one is framed against the same person, and when a conviction has been had on one or more of them, the complainant, or the officer conducting the prosecution, may, with the consent of the Court, withdraw the remaining charge or charges, or the Court of its own accord may stay the inquiry into, or trial of, such charge or charges and such withdrawal shall have the effect of an acquittal on such charge or charges, unless the conviction be set aside, in which case the said Court (subject to the order of the Court setting aside the conviction) may proceed with the inquiry into, or trial of, the charge or charges so withdrawn.

225.title: Trial to be conducted by Public Prosecutor
225.what: In every trial before a Court of Session, the prosecution shall be conducted by a Public Prosecutor.

226.title: Opening case for prosecution
226.what: When the accused appears or is brought before the Court i n pursuance of a commitment of the case under section 209, the prosecutor shall open his case by describing the charge brought against the accused and stating by what evidence he proposes to prove the guilt of the accused.

227.title: Discharge
227.what: If, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution in this behalf, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.

228.title: Framing of charge
228.what: The Judge may frame a charge against the accused and transfer the case for trial to a Chief Judicial Magistrate or any other Judicial Magistrate of the first class if the accused has committed an offence that is not exclusively triable by the Court of Session, or frame a written charge against the accused if it is exclusively triable by the Court. The charge must be read and explained to the accused, who can then plead guilty or claim to be tried.

229.title: Conviction on plea of guilty
229.what: If the accused pleads guilty, the Judge shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon.

230.title: Date for prosecution evidence
230.what: If the accused refuses to plead, or does not plead, or claims to be tried or is not convicted under section 229, the Judge shall fix a date for the examination of witnesses, and may, on the application of the prosecution, issue any process for compelling the attendance of any witness or the production of any document or other thing.

231.title: Evidence for prosecution
231.what: The Judge shall proceed to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution on a fixed date, and may permit cross-examination to be deferred or recall any witness for further cross-examination.

232.title: Acquittal
232.what: If the Judge finds no evidence that the accused committed the offence after taking the evidence for the prosecution, examining the accused, and hearing both the prosecution and defence, the Judge shall record an order of acquittal.

233.title: Entering upon defence
233.what: The accused is called upon to enter on his defence and adduce any evidence he may have in support thereof, and if he puts in a written statement, it shall be filed with the record.

234.title: Arguments
234.what: When the examination of witnesses for the defence is complete, the prosecutor sums up his case, and the accused or his pleader is entitled to reply, with permission from the Judge to make submissions on any point of law raised by the accused.

235.title: Judgment of acquittal or conviction
235.what: Section 235 states that after hearing arguments and points of law, the Judge shall give a judgment in the case. If the accused is convicted, the Judge shall hear the accused on the questions of sentence and then pass sentence according to law.

236.title: Previous conviction
236.what: Section 236 states that if a previous conviction is charged under certain provisions, the Judge may take evidence in respect of the alleged previous conviction after convicting the accused under sections 229 or 235, but only if the accused has been convicted under those sections.

237.title: Procedure in cases instituted under section 199( 2)
237.what: A Court of Session taking cognizance of an offence under sub-section (2) of section 199 shall try the case in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases instituted otherwise than on a police report before a Court of Magistrate: Provided that the person against whom the offence is alleged to have been committed shall, unless the Court of Session, for reasons to be recorded, otherwise directs, be examined as a witness for the prosecution.

238.title: Compliance with section 207
238.what: The Magistrate must ensure the accused complies with Section 207 when appearing in court.

239.title: When accused shall be discharged
239.what: If, upon considering the police report and the documents sent with it under section 173 and making such examination, if any, of the accused as the Magistrate thinks necessary and after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being heard, the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused, and record his reasons for so doing.

240.title: Framing of charge
240.what: STATE AMENDMENT Chhattisgarh In sub-section ( 2) of section 240 of the Principal Act, after the word “to the accused” the following shall be added:— “present either in person or through the medium of electronic video linkage in the presence of his pleader in the Court.” [Vide Chhattisgarh Act 13 of 2006, s. 5].

241.title: Conviction on plea of guilty
241.what: If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon.

242.title: Evidence for prosecution
242.what: (1) If the accused refuses to plead or does not plead, or claims to be tried or the Magistrate does not convict the accused under section 241, the Magistrate shall fix a date for the examination of witnesses: 1[Provided that the Magistrate shall supply in advance to the accused, the statement of witnesses recorded during investigation by the police]. (2) The Magistrate may, on the application of the prosecution, issue a summons to any of its witnesses directing him to attend or to produce any document or other thing. (3) On the date so fixed, the Magistrate shall proceed to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution: Provided that the Magistrate may permit the cross-examination of any witness to be deferred until any other witness or witnesses have been examined or recall any witness for further cross-examination.

243.title: Evidence for defence
243.what: The accused shall then be called upon to enter upon his defence and produce his evidence; and if the accused puts in any written statement, the Magistrate shall file it with the record.

244.title: Evidence for prosecution
244.what: When, in any warrant-case instituted otherwise than on a police report, the accused appears or is brought before a Magistrate, the Magistrate shall proceed to hear the prosecution and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution.

245.title: When accused shall be discharged
245.what: Section 245 states that if a Magistrate considers that no case against an accused has been made out which would warrant conviction, the Magistrate shall discharge the accused, unless the prosecution satisfies the Magistrate that it is not in the interest of justice to do so.

246.title: Procedure where accused is not discharged
246.what: If a Magistrate thinks the accused has committed an offence that can be tried by them and punished adequately, they must frame a written charge against the accused. The charge is then read to the accused, who can plead guilty or make a defence. If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate may convict them. If not, the accused must state which witnesses they want to cross-examine at the next hearing.

247.title: Evidence for defence
247.what: The accused must defend themselves and present their own evidence, with the rules from section 243 applying.

248.title: Acquittal or conviction
248.what: (1) If, in any case under this Chapter in which a charge has been framed, the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal. (2) Where, in any case under this Chapter, the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, but does not proceed in accordance with the provisions of section 325 or section 360, he shall, after hearing the accused on the question of sentence, pass sentence upon him according to law. (3) Where, in any case under this Chapter, a previous conviction is charged under the provisions o f sub-section (7) of section 211 and the accused does not admit that he has been previously convicted as alleged in the charge, the Magistrate may, after he has convicted the said accused, take evidence in respect of the alleged previous conviction, and shall record a finding thereon: Provided that no such charge shall be read out by the Magistrate nor shall the accused be asked to plead thereto nor shall the previous conviction be referred to by the prosecution or in any evidence adduced by it, unless and until the accused has been convicted under sub-section (2).

249.title: Absence of complainant
249.what: When the proceedings have been instituted upon complaint, and on any day fixed for the hearing of the case, the complainant is absent, and the offence may be lawfully compounded or is not a cognizable offence, the Magistrate may, in his discretion, notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, at any time before the charge has been framed, discharge the accused.

250.title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause
250.what: If, in any case instituted upon complaint or upon information given to a police officer or to a Magistrate, one or more persons is or are accused before a Magistrate of any offence triable by a Magistrate, and the Magistrate by whom the case is heard discharges or acquits all or any of the accused, and is of opinion that there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation against them or any of them, the Magistrate may, by his order of discharge or acquittal, if the person upon whose complaint or information the accusation was made is present, call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused or to each or any of such accused when there are more than one; or, if such person is not present, direct the issue of a summons to him to appear and show cause as aforesaid.

251.title: Substance of accusation to be stated
251.what: When in a summons-case the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate, the particulars of the offence of which he is accused shall be stated to him, and he shall be asked whether he pleads guilty or has any defence to make, but it shall not be necessary to frame a formal charge.

252.title: Conviction on plea of guilty
252.what: If the accused pleas guilty, the Magistrate will write down their words exactly or change them slightly to make sense, then convict them.

253.title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases
253.what: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases: The accused shall transmit to the Magistrate a letter containing his plea and the amount of fine specified in the summons, and the Magistrate may convict the accused in his absence, on his plea of guilty and sentence him to pay the fine.

254.title: Procedure when not convicted
254.what: Procedure when not convicted: If the Magistrate does not convict the accused under section 252 or section 253, he shall proceed to hear the prosecution and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution, and also to hear the accused and take all such evidence as he produces in his defence.

255.title: Acquittal or conviction
255.what: If the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal. If the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, he shall pass sentence upon him according to law.

256.title: Non-appearance or death of complainant
256.what: If a person who has filed a complaint does not appear in court on the appointed day or any subsequent day, the Magistrate will acquit the accused unless it's deemed necessary to adjourn the hearing. The Magistrate can decide not to require the complainant's attendance if they are represented by someone else or if their presence is not needed.

257.title: Withdrawal of complaint
257.what: If a complainant, at any time before a final order is passed in any case under this Chapter, satisfies the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for permitting him to withdraw his complaint against the accused, or if there be more than one accused, against all or any of them, the Magistrate may permit him to withdraw the same, and shall thereupon acquit the accused against whom the complaint is so withdrawn.

258.title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases
258.what: In any summons-case instituted otherwise than upon complaint, a Magistrate of the first class or, with the previous sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, any other Judicial Magistrate, may, for reasons to be recorded by him, stop the proceedings at any stage without pronouncing any judgment and where such stoppage of proceedings is made after the evidence of the principal witnesses has been recorded, pronounce a judgment of acquittal, and in any other case, release the accused, and such release shall have the effect of discharge.

259.title: Power of Court to convert summons-cases into warrant-cases
259.what: The Magistrate may proceed to re-hear a summons-case relating to an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases, and may re-call any witness who may have been examined.

260.title: Power to try summarily
260.what: A Chief Judicial Magistrate, Metropolitan Magistrate, or a specially empowered Magistrate can try certain offences summarily if they think it's appropriate, including: theft with property value under 2000 rupees, receiving stolen property, assisting in concealing stolen property, and certain other crimes.

261.title: Summary trial by Magistrate of the second class
261.what: The High Court may confer on any Magistrate invested with the powers of a Magistrate of the second class power to try summarily any offence which is punishable only with fine or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months with or without fine, and any abetment of or attempt to commit any such offence.

262.title: Procedure for summary trials
262.what: In trials under this Chapter, the procedure specified in this Code for the trial of summons-case shall be followed except as hereinafter mentioned. No sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding three months shall be passed in the case of any conviction under this Chapter.

263.title: Record in summary trials
263.what: In every case tried summarily, the Magistrate shall enter, in such form as the State Government may direct, the following particulars, namely:— (a) the serial number of the case; (b) the date of the commission of the offence; (c) the date of the report or complaint; (d) the name of the complainant (if any); (e) the name, parentage and residence of the accused; (f) the offence complained of and the offence (if any) proved, and in cases coming under clause (ii), clause (iii) or clause (iv) of s ub-section (1) of section 260, the value of the property in respect of which the offence has been committed; (g) the plea of the accused and his examination (if any); (h) the finding; (i) the sentence or other final order; (j) the date on which proceedings terminated.

264.title: Judgment in cases tried summarily
264.what: The Magistrate shall record the substance of the evidence and a judgment containing a brief statement of the reasons for the finding.

265.title: Language of record and judgment
265.what: Every record and judgment shall be written in the language of the Court. The High Court may authorise any Magistrate to prepare the record or judgment by means of an officer appointed in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and the record or judgment so prepared shall be signed by such Magistrate.

265A.title: Application of the Chapter
265A.what: This Chapter applies in respect of an accused against whom a report has been forwarded alleging an offence other than one for which the punishment of death or imprisonment for life or exceeding seven years has been provided under the law, and does not apply where the offence affects the socio-economic condition of the country or has been committed against a woman or child below 14 years.

265B.title: Application for plea bargaining
265B.what: A person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining in the Court in which such offence is pending for trial.

265C.title: Guidelines for mutually satisfactory disposition
265C.what: The Court shall follow a specific procedure when working out a mutually satisfactory disposition under section 265B: In cases instituted on police report, all parties must attend a meeting. In other cases, only the accused and victim must attend a meeting.

265D.title: Report of the mutually satisfactory disposition to be submitted before the Court
265D.what: Where in a meeting under section 265C, a satisfactory disposition of the case has been worked out, the Court shall prepare a report of such disposition which shall be signed by the presiding officer of the Court and all other persons who participated in the meeting and if no such disposition has been worked out, the Court shall record such observation and proceed further in accordance with the provisions of this Code from the stage the application under sub-section (1) of section 265B has been filed in such case.

265E.title: Disposal of the case
265E.what: The Court shall dispose of the case by awarding compensation to the victim and hearing parties on punishment, probation, or release, following specific procedures.

265F.title: Judgment of the Court
265F.what: The Court shall deliver its judgment in terms of section 265E in the open Court and the same shall be signed by the presiding officer of the Court.

265G.title: Finality of the judgment
265G.what: The judgment delivered by the Court is final, with no appeals allowed except for certain petitions.

265H.title: Power of the Court in plea bargaining
265H.what: A Court shall have, for the purposes of discharging its functions under this Chapter, all the powers vested in respect of bail, trial of offences and other matters relating to the disposal of a case in such Court under this Code.

265J.title: Savings
265J.what: The provisions of this Chapter shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other provisions of this Code and nothing in such other provisions shall be construed to constrain the meaning of any provision of this Chapter.

265K.title: Statements of accused not to be used
265K.what: Notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, the statements or facts stated by an accused in an application for plea bargaining filed under section 265B shall not be used for any other purpose except for the purpose of this Chapter.

265L.title: Non-application of the Chapter
265L.what: Nothing in this Chapter applies to juveniles or children as defined in clause (k) of section 2 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

266.title: Definitions
266.what: This Chapter defines key terms such as 'detained' and 'prison', including subsidiary jails and reformatory institutions.

268.title: Power of State Government to exclude certain persons from operation of section 267
268.what: The State Government has the power to exclude certain persons from the operation of section 267 by issuing a general or special order.

269.title: Officer in charge of prison to abstain from carrying out order in certain contingencies
269.what: The officer in charge of a prison must not carry out an order if the person is: sick/infirm, under trial/remand, or will be released before the order can be carried out. If this happens, they must send a statement to the court explaining why.

270.title: Prisoner to be brought to Court in custody
270.what: The officer in charge of the prison must bring the prisoner to court in custody and keep them there until they are examined or released back to prison

271.title: Power to issue commission for examination of witness in prison
271.what: The provisions of this Chapter shall be without prejudice to the power of the Court to issue, under section 284, a commission for the examination, as a witness, of any person confined or detained in a prison; and the provisions of Part B of Chapter XXIII shall apply in relation to the examination on commission of any such person in the prison as they apply in relation to the examination on commission of any other person.

272.title: Language of Courts
272.what: The State Government may determine what shall be, for purposes of this Code, the language of each Court within the State other than the High Court.

273.title: Evidence to be taken in presence of accused
273.what: All evidence taken in the course of a trial or other proceeding must be taken in the presence of the accused, or with their pleader present, unless otherwise expressly provided.

274.title: Record in summons-cases and inquiries
274.what: The Magistrate must make a written record of the evidence presented during a summons-case, inquiry, or other proceedings, unless they are unable to do so themselves.
274.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

275.title: Record in warrant-cases
275.what: In all warrant-cases tried before a Magistrate, the evidence of each witness shall, as his examination proceeds, be taken down in writing either by the Magistrate himself or by his dictation in open Court or, where he is unable to do so owing to a physical or other incapacity, under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed by him in this behalf.
275.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

276.title: Record in trial before Court of Session
276.what: The evidence of each witness shall be taken down in writing by the presiding Judge or his dictation, or under his direction and superintendence by an officer of the Court.
276.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

277.title: Language of record of evidence
277.what: In every case where evidence is taken down under section 275 or 276,— (a) if the witness gives evidence in the language of the Court, it shall be taken down in that language; (b) if he gives evidence in any other language, it may, if practicable, be taken down in that language, and if it is not practicable to do so, a true translation of the evidence in the language of the Court shall be prepared as the examination of the witness proceeds, signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge, and shall form part of the record; (c) where under clause (b) evidence is taken down in a language other than the language of the Court, a true translation thereof in the language of the Court shall be prepared as soon as practicable, signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge, and shall form part of the record: Provided that when under clause ( b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties, the Court may dispense with such translation.
277.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

278.title: Procedure in regard to such evidence when completed
278.what: The evidence of each witness taken under sections 275 or 276 shall be read over to the accused in attendance or his pleader if he appears by pleader, and may be corrected if necessary. If a witness objects to any part of the evidence, the Magistrate or Judge may make a memorandum of the objection and add remarks as needed. If the record is in a language different from the one given, it shall be interpreted for the witness in that language or a language they understand.
278.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

279.title: Interpretation of evidence to accused or his pleader
279.what: Whenever any evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused, and he is present in Court in person, it shall be interpreted to him in open Court in a language understood by him. If he appears by pleader and the evidence is given in a language other than the language of the Court, and not understood by the pleader, it shall be interpreted to such pleader in that language. When documents are put for the purpose of formal proof, it shall be in the discretion of the Court to interpret as much thereof as appears necessary.
279.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

280.title: Remarks respecting demeanour of witness
280.what: When a presiding Judge or Magistrate has recorded the evidence of a witness, he shall also record such remarks (if any) as he thinks material respecting the demeanour of such witness whilst under examination.
280.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

281.title: Record of examination of accused
281.what: Section 281 states that when an accused is examined by a Metropolitan Magistrate, the Magistrate must make a memorandum of the examination in the language of the Court and sign it, which shall form part of the record. When an accused is examined by any other Magistrate or Court, the whole examination must be recorded in full by the presiding Judge or Magistrate, who may appoint an officer to assist with recording if needed.
281.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

282.title: Interpreter to be bound to interpret truthfully
282.what: An interpreter must accurately convey the meaning of evidence or statements in court.
282.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

283.title: Record in High Court
283.what: Every High Court may prescribe a rule for taking down evidence of witnesses and examining the accused.
283.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

284.title: When attendance of witness may be dispensed with and commission issued
284.what: Whenever, in the course of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, it appears to a Court or Magistrate that the examination of a witness is necessary for the ends of justice, and that the attendance of such witness cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which, under the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable, the Court or Magistrate may dispense with such attendance and may issue a commission for the examination of the witness in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter: Provided that where the examination of the President or the Vice-President of India or the Governor of a State or the Administrator of a Union territory as a witness is necessary for the ends of Justice, a commission shall be issued for the examination of such a witness. (2) The Court may, when issuing a commission for the examination of a witness for the prosecution, direct that such amount as the Court considers reasonable to meet the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees, be paid by the prosecution.
284.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

285.title: Commission to whom to be issued
285.what: The commission shall be directed to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate, as the case may be, within whose local jurisdiction the witness is to be found if the witness is within the territories to which this Code extends. If the witness is in India, but in a State or an area to which this Code does not extend, the commission shall be directed to such Court or officer as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.
285.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

286.title: Execution of commissions
286.what: The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, or Chief Judicial Magistrate, or a designated Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate, must summon a witness before them or visit their location to take their evidence, exercising the same powers as during trials or warrant cases.
286.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

287.title: Parties may examine witnesses
287.what: Parties to a proceeding can ask questions of witnesses in writing, and the court or magistrate can then ask those questions to the witness.
287.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

288.title: Return of commission
288.what: A commission issued under section 284 must be returned to the Court or Magistrate issuing it, along with the witness's deposition, which can be inspected and read in evidence at any time
288.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

289.title: Adjournment of proceeding
289.what: In every case in which a commission is issued under section 284, the inquiry, trial or other proceeding may be adjourned for a specified time reasonably sufficient for the execution and return of the commission.
289.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

290.title: Execution of foreign commissions
290.what: The provisions of section 286 and so much of section 287 and section 288 as relate to the execution of a commission and its return shall apply in respect of commissions issued by any of the Courts, Judges or Magistrates hereinafter mentioned as they apply to commissions issued under section 284.
290.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

291.title: Deposition of medical witness
291.what: This section states that the deposition of a medical witness can be given in evidence in any inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under this Code, even if the deponent is not called as a witness.
291.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

291A.title: Identification report of Magistrate
291A.what: Any document purporting to be a report of identification under an Executive Magistrate's hand can be used as evidence in court proceedings, but certain statements may not be admissible without following specific Indian Evidence Act provisions.
291A.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

292.title: Evidence of officers of the Mint
292.what: Any document purporting to be a report under the hand of an officer of the Mint or of any Note Printing Press or of any Security Printing Press (including the officer of the Controller of Stamps and Stationery) or of any Forensic Department or Division of Forensic Science Laboratory or any Government Examiner of Questioned Documents or any State Examiner of Questioned Documents, as the case may be, upon any matter or thing duly submitted to him for examination and report in the course of any proceeding under this Code, may be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, although such officer is not called as a witness.
292.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

293.title: Reports of certain Government scientific experts
293.what: A document from a government scientific expert's report can be used as evidence in court proceedings if it was submitted for examination and analysis.
293.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

294.title: No formal proof of certain documents
294.what: Section 294 states that when a document is filed before any court, the prosecution or accused must admit or deny the genuineness of each document, and the list of documents shall be in a form prescribed by the State Government.
294.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

295.title: Affidavit in proof of conduct of public servants
295.what: Section 295 allows public servants to give evidence of facts alleged in an application by affidavit, and the court may order that such evidence be given if it thinks fit.
295.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

296.title: Evidence of formal character on affidavit
296.what: The evidence of any person whose evidence is of a formal character may be given by affidavit and may, subject to all just exceptions, be read in evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code.
296.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

297.title: Authorities before whom affidavits may be sworn
297.what: Affidavits to be used before any Court under this Code may be sworn or affirmed before any Judge or Judicial or Executive Magistrate, or any Commissioner of Oaths appointed by a High Court or Court of Session, or any notary appointed under the Notaries Act, 1952.
297.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

298.title: Previous conviction or acquittal how proved
298.what: A previous conviction or acquittal may be proved in an inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under this Code by an extract certified under the hand of the officer having the custody of the records of the Court in which such conviction or acquittal was held, or by a certificate signed by the officer in charge of the Jail in which the punishment or any part thereof was undergone.
298.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

299.title: Record of evidence in absence of accused
299.what: If an accused person absconding is to be tried, the court may examine witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution and record their depositions, which can be given in evidence against the accused if the witness is dead, incapable, or cannot be found without unreasonable delay, expense, or inconvenience.
299.chapter: Chapter VIII has been commenced under this Code.

300.title: Person once convicted or acquitted not to be tried for same offence
300.what: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence, nor on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge from the one made against him might have been made under sub-section (1) of section 221, or for which he might have been convicted under sub-section (2) thereof.

301.title: Appearance by Public Prosecutors
301.what: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case may appear and plead without any written authority before any Court in which that case is under inquiry, trial or appeal.

302.title: Permission to conduct prosecution
302.what: Any Magistrate inquiring into or trying a case may permit the prosecution to be conducted by any person other than a police officer below the rank of inspector; but no person, other than the Advocate-General or Government Advocate or a Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor, shall be entitled to do so without such permission.

303.title: Right of person against whom proceedings are instituted to be defended
303.what: Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or against whom proceedings are instituted under this Code, may of right be defended by a pleader of his choice.

304.title: Legal aid to accused at State expense in certain cases
304.what: (1) Where, in a trial before the Court of Session, the accused is not represented by a pleader, and where it appears to the Court that the accused has not sufficient means to engage a pleader, the Court shall assign a pleader for his defence at the expense of the State. (2) The High Court may, with the previous approval of the State Government, make rules providing for— (a) the mode of selecting pleaders for defence under sub-section (1); (b) the facilities to be allowed to such pleaders by the Courts; (c) the fees payable to such pleaders by the Government, and generally, for carrying out the purposes of sub-section (1). (3) The State Government may, by notification, direct that, as from such date as may be specified in the notification, the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) shall apply in relation to any class of trials before other Courts in the State as they apply in relation to trials before Courts of Session.

305.title: Procedure when corporation or registered society is an accused
305.what: This section outlines the procedure for corporations and registered societies when they are accused in an inquiry or trial, including the appointment of representatives and the application of certain requirements to these representatives.

306.title: Tender of pardon to accomplice
306.what: This section states that with a view to obtaining the evidence of any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in or privy to an offence to which this section applies, the Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Metropolitan Magistrate at any stage of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of, the offence, and the Magistrate of the first class inquiring into or trying the offence, at any stage of the inquiry or trial, may tender a pardon to such person on condition of his making a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the commission thereof.

307.title: Power to direct tender of pardon
307.what: The Court can offer a pardon to someone who has been committed for an offense before judgment is passed, with the goal of getting them to testify at trial about their involvement in the crime.

308.title: Trial of person not complying with conditions of pardon
308.what: Section 308 states that a person who has accepted a tender of pardon may be tried for the offence in respect of which the pardon was made or for any other offence of which they appear to have been guilty in connection with the same matter, and also for the offence of giving false evidence.

309.title: Power to postpone or adjourn proceedings
309.what:
Section 309 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the procedure for postponing or adjourning court proceedings. Key aspects include: 

- The Court may postpone or adjourn proceedings from day-to-day until all witnesses are examined unless it finds adjournment necessary for reasons to be recorded.

- In cases related to certain offenses (sections 376, 376A, 376B, 376C, 376D, 376DA, and 376DB of the Indian Penal Code), proceedings must be completed within two months from the date of filing the charge sheet.

- The Court can postpone or adjourn proceedings for reasons to be recorded, with reasonable terms and time.

- No Magistrate can remand an accused person to custody for more than 15 days at a time.

- Adjournments are not granted without examining witnesses unless special reasons are recorded in writing.

- No adjournment is allowed solely to enable the accused to show cause against the proposed sentence.

- Adjournments are not granted at the request of a party except in exceptional circumstances, such as the witness being engaged in another court or the party's pleader being unavailable.

- The Court may record the statement of a witness if they are present but the party or their pleader is not ready to examine or cross-examine them.

- The court may postpone or adjourn proceedings for a maximum period of six months from the date of filing of the charge sheet.

310.title: Local inspection
310.what: A Judge or Magistrate may visit and inspect any place relevant to an inquiry or trial, recording a memorandum of facts observed, which forms part of the case record.

311.title: Power to summon material witness, or examine person present
311.what: A Court can summon or examine any person present, including those not summoned as witnesses, if their evidence is deemed essential for the case's just decision.

311A.title: Power of Magistrate to order person to give specimen signatures or handwriting
311A.what: A Magistrate of the first class may direct a person to give specimen signatures or handwriting if it is expedient for an investigation or proceeding under this Code, and the person has been arrested in connection with such investigation or proceeding.

312.title: Expenses of complainants and witnesses
312.what: A Criminal Court may order payment of reasonable expenses of complainants or witnesses attending for purposes of inquiry, trial, or other proceedings under this Code, subject to rules made by the State Government.

313.title: Power to examine the accused
313.what: The court may put questions to the accused at any stage without warning, and shall question him generally on the case after the prosecution witnesses have been examined, except in summons cases where personal attendance is dispensed with.

314.title: Oral arguments and memorandum of arguments
314.what: A party can give oral arguments and submit a written memorandum after presenting evidence, which must be part of the record. The opposing party must receive a copy of the written memorandum. The Court may delay filing written arguments if it deems them unnecessary.

315.title: Accused person to be competent witness
315.what: Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court shall be a competent witness for the defence and may give evidence on oath in disproof of the charges made against him or any person charged together with him at the same trial, provided that he shall not be called as a witness except on his own request in writing.

316.title: No influence to be used to induce disclosure
316.what: No one can use promises, threats, or other means to get a person who is accused of a crime to tell more or less than they know about the case.

317.title: Provision for inquiries and trial being held in the absence of accused in certain cases
317.what: Section 317 states that a Judge or Magistrate may dispense with the personal attendance of an accused in certain cases if they are satisfied that it is not necessary for justice, and may direct their attendance at any subsequent stage of proceedings.

318.title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings
318.what: Section 318 outlines the procedure to be followed when an accused cannot understand the proceedings, allowing the Court to proceed with the inquiry or trial and forwarding the case to a High Court if necessary.

319.title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence
319.what: The court can proceed against other persons appearing guilty of an offence, and they can be arrested or summoned based on the circumstances of the case.

320.title: Compounding of offences
320.what: Section 320 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the compounding of offences. According to this section, a person can compound certain offences with the permission of a court, except in cases where the accused is under 18 years old, an idiot, or a lunatic. The legal representative of a deceased person can also compound the offence with the consent of the court. In other cases, composition for the offence is allowed only if the accused has not been committed for trial or convicted and an appeal is pending. A High Court or Court of Session can allow a person to compound an offence if they are competent to do so under this section. The composition of an offence has the effect of an acquittal for the accused. No offence can be compounded if the accused is liable for enhanced punishment or a different kind of punishment due to a previous conviction.

321.title: Withdrawal from prosecution
321.what: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case may withdraw from the prosecution of any person either generally or in respect of one or more offences with the consent of the Court before judgment is pronounced, and upon such withdrawal, the accused shall be discharged or acquitted depending on whether a charge has been framed or not.

322.title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of
322.what: If a Magistrate appears to warrant a presumption that he lacks jurisdiction to try a case or commit it for trial, he may stay proceedings and submit the case to a higher authority with jurisdiction, who can then decide whether to try the case themselves or refer it to another Magistrate.
322.chapter: Part II of Section 506 The person against whom the

323.title: Procedure when, after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be
323.what: If a Magistrate finds that a case should be tried by the Court of Session, they will transfer it to that court and follow the rules for transferring cases.
323.chapter: Part II of Section 506 The person against whom the

324.what: Where a person, having been convicted of an offence punishable under Chapter XII or Chapter XVII of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards, is again accused of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards, and

325.title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe
325.what: Whenever a Magistrate is of opinion, after hearing the evidence for the prosecution and the accused, that the accused is guilty, and that he ought to receive a punishment different in kind from, or more severe than, that which such Magistrate is empowered to inflict, or, being a Magistrate of the second class, is of opinion that the accused ought to be required to execute a bond under section 106, he may record the opinion and submit his proceedings, and forward the accused, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate to whom he is subordinate.

326.what: When a case is transferred, the new judge/magistrate can act on previously recorded evidence from the previous judge/magistrate, but may re-examine witnesses if necessary.

327.title: Court to be open
327.what: The place in which any Criminal Court is held for the purpose of inquiring into or trying any offence shall be deemed to be an open Court, to which the public generally may have access, so far as the same can conveniently contain them: Provided that the presiding Judge or Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, order at any stage of any inquiry into, or trial of, any particular case, that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access to, or be or remain in, the room or building used by the Court.
